title: TB4-08044
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXthe Appellant), a citizen of El Salvador, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXthe Appellant), a citizen of El Salvador, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection. He has submitted new evidence in support of his appeal. The Appellant asks the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to accept the new evidence in accordance to Section 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protections Act (IRPA), set aside the Board's decision and to refer the matter back to the RPD for a new hearing by a different member and to include the issue of "inclusion" in that hearing or to set an oral hearing in accordance to Section 110(6) of the IRPA.
Pursuant to Section 111(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD refers the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel. Background

The Appellant alleged before the RPD that he fears the gang known as the MS13, in El Salvador as well as in the U.S.A. Full details of his allegations are available in his Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative. The Appellant fled El Salvador in 2000, going to the U.S.A. where he held temporary protected status. He re-availed in 2008 and left again after learning the gang was still after him. He left the U.S.A. for Canada after receiving threatening phone calls there. He crossed into Canada without reporting to the Canada Border Services but was arrested sometime later on an outstanding U.S. warrant.

The Appellant's application for refugee protection was brought before the Board for his hearing on May 14, 2014. During that hearing, the only issue discussed was in regards to the possible exclusion of the Appellant in accordance to Article 1F(b) of the 1951 Convention and the 1967 Protocol relating to the Status of Refugees (the Convention) which is articulated clearly in the United Nations High Commission for Refugees (UNHCR) handbook.1 In listening to the audio tape, the RAD notes that there occurred a detailed pre-hearing discussion amongst the counsels for the Appellant, counsel for the Minister and the Panel regarding an agreed upon statement of facts, exclusion, whether to allow witness testimony on the exclusion, the law as it applies in Canada, the law as it was applied in XXXX and much more. Some of this discussion was had without the presence of the Appellant; however, the Appellant was present for much of it, including the portions of the hearing in which the issue of possible witnesses were discussed. The Panel made it clear on a number of occasions during this part of the hearing that there would be no re-trial of the conviction in XXXX.

At the end of the morning, the Panel requested written submissions form both counsels in regards to one question to be considered by the Panel. The Panel asked "Should the Panel consider and take into account potential defenses which the claimant may have had and used, if he had been charged in Canada with the equivalent act?" This question was in relation to the Article 1F(b) exclusion. The Panel and counsels agreed on dates for submissions and the Panel laid out tentative plans for what may occur once he had made his decision on the submissions and subsequently on the exclusion issue.

Subsequently, the panel issued his decision on August 21, 2014, excluding the claimant under Article 1F(b) : a) The Appellant submits that the RPD erred by failing to allow the Appellant any opportunity to present evidence, question witnesses and to make final presentations. b) The Appellant submits that the RPD made numerous findings of fact without ever questioning the witness. c) The Appellant submits that he was denied the legal right to put his case forward. d) The Appellant submits that the RPD recognized at the hearing that the matter was not yet completed but made and wrote its decision regardless of that recognition. e) The Appellant submits that the RPD breached the Appellant's right to procedural fairness and violated the doctrine of legitimate expectations by denying him the right to testify. f) The Appellant submits that the RPD made several errors in its decision by referencing to the Appellant's "oral testimony." The Appellant submits he never gave oral testimony. g) The Appellant submits that the RPD made gross misrepresentations of the Appellant and his common law spouse's relationship and the Panel's disapproval of the Appellant's actions is clearly obvious in his decision. h) The Appellant submits that the RPD erred when it failed to do a separate analysis under Section 97 of the IRPA.

The Appellant requests that the RAD grant this appeal and that it refer the matter back to the RPD for a new hearing with s different panel, or in the alternative, the Appellant asks the RAD to order that the Appellant is not excluded from refugee protection and a new hearing by the RPD be held on the inclusion case. ANALYSIS Admissibility of Evidence Submitted on Appeal

Section 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the Appellant may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of his claim or that was not reasonably available, or that he could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

Even where a document meets the test in Section 110(4), this does not require the RAD to admit it into evidence without any further consideration. It is for the Appellant to make full and detailed submissions in his Memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of Section 110(4) and how that evidence relates to the Appellant.2

In Raza, paragraph 16, the Federal Court of Appeal endorsed the principle that a document's "newness" cannot be tested solely by its date of creation; what is important is the event or circumstance sought to be proved by the evidence.

In regards to this appeal, two affidavits were disclosed in the Appellant's record which the RAD can find no mention of in regards to Rule 29 of the RAD rules. Further, there is no mention of these affidavits in the Memorandum, either. However, in an effort to be as fair as possible, the RAD will look at these and make a decision on their admissibility in accordance to Section 110(4) of the IRPA.

The first affidavit is one from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, a lawyer at the law office of XXXX XXXX (counsel of record for the Appellant). In this affidavit, Ms. XXXX attests to the facts regarding the hearing of May 16, 2014 including, after she listened to the official recording of that proceeding, an exchange in which the Panel confirmed that he would communicate in writing his decision on whether he will allow testimony from the family members. Further, she attests to the point that at no point in the recording does the panel state that the hearing was completed and that he would be making his final decision.

Is this affidavit "new"? The RAD finds that it is not new, as it deals only with the recorded record of the hearing which occurred on May 16, 2014. There is nothing new in the affidavit and the content of the affidavit itself is not material because it only reiterates what was on the official record. This affidavit will be disallowed.

The second affidavit comes from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, also a lawyer at Ms. XXXX firm. In this affidavit, Ms. XXXX attests to the content of conversations between Ms. XXXX and the counsel for the Minister, Mr. Klaus. Ms. XXXX heard none of the conversations related to in the affidavit but is only attesting to what she was told afterwards by Ms. XXXX.

The document is new and does speak to conversations which occurred after the hearing so in that regard, it may be considered under Section 110(4) as allowable. Even though the RAD can give less weight to such hearsay evidence, the affidavit will be allowed and considered by the RAD. Role of the RAD

Counsel has made some submissions in regard to the role that the RAD plays in the review of an RPD decision. However, the RAD finds that the recent Federal Court decision, in Huruglica,3 provides the RAD with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal such as the RAD to decisions of a first-level administrative tribunal. Justice Phelan states in paragraphs 54 and 55 of the foregoing decision: [54] Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision. [55] In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an "overriding and palpable error."

Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its own assessment of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the Appellant should be excluded in accordance to Article 1F(b). The RPD's Findings

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by failing to allow the Appellant any opportunity to present evidence, question witnesses and to make final presentations. The RPD was required to look at the Minister's request for exclusion before any hearing of inclusion could occur.

101. (1) A claim is ineligible to be referred to the Refugee Protection Division if a) refugee protection has been conferred on the claimant under this Act; b) a claim for refugee protection by the claimant has been rejected by the Board; c) a prior claim by the claimant was determined to be ineligible to be referred to the Refugee Protection Division, or to have been withdrawn or abandoned; d) the claimant has been recognized as a Convention refugee by a country other than Canada and can be sent or returned to that country; e) the claimant came directly or indirectly to Canada from a country designated by the regulations, other than a country of their nationality or their former habitual residence; or f) the claimant has been determined to be inadmissible on grounds of security, violating human or international rights, serious criminality or organized criminality, except for persons who are inadmissible solely on the grounds of paragraph 35(1)(c). (2) A claim is not ineligible by reason of serious criminality under paragraph (1)(f) unless a) in the case of inadmissibility by reason of a conviction in Canada, the conviction is for an offence under an Act of Parliament punishable by a maximum term of imprisonment of at least 10 years; or b) in the case of inadmissibility by reason of a conviction outside Canada, the conviction is for an offence that, if committed in Canada, would constitute an offence under an Act of Parliament punishable by a maximum term of imprisonment of at least 10 years.

In this particular appeal, the facts are laid out before the RAD as follows: 1) The Appellant pleaded guilty in an XXXX court to "Sexual Assault 4th Degree".4 The elements of such a charge and this one in particular are that a) the accused is twenty years of age or older, b) the accused engaged in sexual intercourse with a person who is c) less than 16 years of age and d) who is not the person's spouse. 2) The Appellant pled guilty to this offense based on those elements listed above.
In summary, the Appellant pleaded guilty to having sexual intercourse with a person under the age of 16 who was not the Appellant's spouse, while he was over the age of 20.

What the RAD must consider now is whether or not the conviction in XXXX would be treated differently in Canada. Counsel for the Appellant argues that in Canada, there would not even be any charges laid as the so-called victim was in fact the Appellant's spouse. The Minister argued at the RPD that the plea bargain agreed to by the Appellant in XXXX acknowledges on his part that the "victim" was not his spouse at the time of the assault and at the time of the conviction (the RAD recognizes that the Appellant disagrees with referring to the female in question as a victim).
The Appellant argues that the RPD breached natural justice when it failed to allow the Appellant an opportunity to testify, to have witnesses heard and to present evidence in support of his case.
The RAD has considered this carefully and has also considered the "doctrine of legitimate expectations." Natural Justice

The only issue that the RAD needs to deal with at this point is the issue of natural justice. It is written in Jayasekara5 by the Hon. Justice Letourneau, that: "I believe there is a consensus among the courts that the interpretation of the exclusion clause in Article 1F(b) of the Convention, as regards the seriousness of a crime, requires an evaluation of the elements of the crime, the mode of prosecution, the penalty prescribed, the facts and the mitigating and aggravating circumstances underlying the conviction (UNDERLINE AND ITALICS HERE ARE THE RADS) see S. v. Refugee Status Appeals Authority; S.& Ors v. Secretary of State for the Home Department, [2006] EWCA Civ 1157; Miguel-Miguel v. Gonzales, 500 F.3d 941 (9th Cir. 2007), August 29, 2007, at pages 945 and 946-947. In other words, whatever presumption of seriousness may attach to a crime internationally or under the legislation of the receiving state, that presumption may be rebutted by reference to the above factors. There is no balancing, however, with factors extraneous to the facts and circumstances underlying the conviction such as, for example, the risk of persecution in the state of origin: see Xie v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FCA 250 (CanLII), [2005] 1 F.C.R. 304 (F.C.A.), at paragraph 38; Immigration and Naturalization Service v. Aguirre-Aguirre, at page 427; T. v. Secretary of State for the Home Department, [1995] 1 W.L.R. 545 (C.A.), at pages 554-555; Dhayakpa v. Minister of Immigration and Ethnic Affairs, at paragraph 24.

The RAD believes that this requirement to evaluate the elements of the crime, etc., requires the RPD to allow the Appellant to testify to and have witnesses testify to the elements of the crime. No proper and complete evaluation can be made without hearing from the Appellant and his witnesses.

The RAD has listened to the recording of the hearing of May 16, 2014. Even though the panel worked very hard at bringing all parties to an understanding of the issues, the two things that were left out of the hearing was the Appellant's testimony and the Appellant's right to make final submissions on the exclusion. The Panel clearly did not allow testimony at the hearing. The Panel ended the recording by suggesting there would be time later for submissions from the Appellant regarding mitigating factors, etc. in the exclusion. A tentative hearing date was set but the date did not work for some parties and before the next hearing date could be set, the Panel reached his decision on exclusion and rendered it in writing to the Appellant, excluding him without ever allowing the Appellant to speak to his own exclusion hearing.

Counsel for the Appellant argues that the Panel disallowed testimony at the hearing despite the Appellant's request. This refusal was an error on the part of the Panel. By refusing to allow the Appellant to present arguments and testimony at the hearing on exclusion, the RPD did breach natural justice and for that reason, the decision cannot stand. Disposition
The RAD has found that the RPD did breach natural justice by not allowing the Appellant to testify or to have witnesses heard or to make final submissions at the hearing of his exclusion issue.

Pursuant to Section 111(1) (c) of IRPA, the RAD refers the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel.
